brief.topic: A Crescent Is a Relationship with Light

s01: The crescent is not a piece missing from the Moon.
It is a meeting between light and a point of view.
The whole sphere is still there.
In this simple model, sunlight illuminates half the sphere.
We see another half: the side facing Earth.
The visible phase is where those two halves overlap.
As the Moon travels around Earth, that overlap changes.
Near the direction of the Sun, the illuminated side faces mostly away from us.
A little farther around, a crescent enters our view.
At a quarter of the cycle, we see half of the bright side.
The visible disk is half lit.
Yet sunlight still covers half of the whole sphere.
On the opposite side of Earth, the bright side faces us.
The disk looks full.
The Moon has not started making more light.
We are seeing more of its sunlit half.
Ordinary phases are not made by Earth casting a shadow.
Earth shadow causes a lunar eclipse, a different alignment.
The real orbit is tilted, so eclipses do not happen every month.
The boundary between day and night is a circle on this ideal sphere.
Seen at an angle, that boundary projects into a curved edge.
Seen edge on, it becomes a straight line across the disk.
This drawing shows illuminated area, not a realistic brightness map.
The familiar shapes return in a cycle of about twenty nine and a half days.
One unchanged sphere, and a slowly changing relationship with light.

scenes.narration:
The crescent is not a piece missing from the Moon. It is a meeting between light and a point of view. The whole sphere is still there.

In this simple model, sunlight illuminates half the sphere. We see another half: the side facing Earth. The visible phase is where those two halves overlap. As the Moon travels around Earth, that overlap changes.

Near the direction of the Sun, the illuminated side faces mostly away from us. A little farther around, a crescent enters our view. At a quarter of the cycle, we see half of the bright side. The visible disk is half lit. Yet sunlight still covers half of the whole sphere.

On the opposite side of Earth, the bright side faces us. The disk looks full. The Moon has not started making more light. We are seeing more of its sunlit half. Ordinary phases are not made by Earth casting a shadow. Earth shadow causes a lunar eclipse, a different alignment. The real orbit is tilted, so eclipses do not happen every month.

The boundary between day and night is a circle on this ideal sphere. Seen at an angle, that boundary projects into a curved edge. Seen edge on, it becomes a straight line across the disk. This drawing shows illuminated area, not a realistic brightness map. The familiar shapes return in a cycle of about twenty nine and a half days. One unchanged sphere, and a slowly changing relationship with light.
